strengths: The paper is easy to follow and for the most part well‑written.
While the paper does not propose novel methods for robustness, it leads an important discussion on the interplay of pre‑trained networks with training methods for group‑robustness.

It provides a novel characterization of distribution shifts and argues about the complementary utility of the two approaches around this characterization, with some theoretical and empirical insights.
The reviewer believes that such an analysis paper is needed in light of recent advances in the studied literature and that the authors have identified well that this is a topic of interest.
The reviewer appreciates the careful discussion in defining and designing in‑support and out‑of‑support shifts, and they believe it is a potentially useful axis of discussion.

The paper addresses the very interesting topic of exploring whether pre‑training helps training performant models under different types of distribution shift, an important frontier in the increasingly adopted pre‑training fine‑tuning methodology.
The ideas presented seem original and the relevant literature is sufficiently discussed.
The later sections on developing more robust models were interesting case studies on how to apply the insights from previous sections.
The problem being investigated is definitely of interest, especially with the emergence of foundation models and the impact of pre‑training data on downstream processes.
This paper is well‑contextualized and its technical structure is plausible (intuitions, motivating examples, formal analysis, generalization, empirical verification, etc.).
The focus of the paper is practically very relevant.
The presentation is somewhat easy to follow.
weaknesses: The design of several experiments is flawed and does not lead to the authors’ claims, constituting a large enough body of the paper to lean towards possible acceptance.

In Section 4/Figure 3, multiple variables are ablated at the same time and the measured effective robustness is with respect to ResNet‑18 models, while the pretrained models compared to have various architectures, making it impossible to isolate the effect of pre‑training alone.

It is unclear whether the perceived robustness is due to purely transfer properties from pretraining strategies or from larger model size, and a comparison should be made between models of the same architecture, with and without pre‑training.

Biased datasets are also susceptible to an in‑support/out‑of‑support analysis, but such an analysis is not given; the paper should explore systematic generalization tasks with missing groups to see how pre‑training’s effectiveness changes as training data becomes more biased.

In Section 5/Figure 5, the first correlation estimate is not strong enough to indicate negative correlation (i) and the authors should provide a confidence interval; the correlation of (ii) is poorly motivated and may be tautologically positive, requiring clarification of why it is meaningful beyond a mathematical identity.

In Section 6, the proposed curated dataset omits the spurious feature (gender) entirely, making the transfer problem an extrapolation one, and the authors need to ablate the impact of aggressive filtering versus counterfactual data generation to show which component is necessary.

The setup for Theorem 3.1 is not presented well; it is unclear why the logistic regression assumption is needed, the proof is not referenced in the main paper, and $proj_{W_{ref}}$ is never formally introduced.
Figure 1’s legend is unreadable due to overlapping text and should be fixed.

Figure 3 lacks an ablation on shift intensity; the influence of shift type, bias strength, and degree of extrapolation on results is not explored, and in‑support and out‑of‑support shifts are not formally defined.
The negative correlation reported in the middle panel of Figure 5 is weak (‑0.112), suggesting that margin gains are independent rather than complementary.

The overall take‑away message is unclear; the paper suggests pre‑training is always desirable but also acknowledges possible harmful biases, making it hard to determine when pre‑training should be used in practice.

The paper is a difficult read; many technical details are missing or inconsistent (e.g., missing key definitions, no details for important procedures, only providing references with no description), rendering many arguments ungrounded and hardly convincing.

Theorem 1 has $w_{ref}$ undefined, and the conclusion that pre‑training/initialization affects ID but not OOD is problematic; conditions under which pre‑training helps, hurts, or does not affect performance are not specified.
Theorem 1 assumes a deterministic model, ignoring stochasticity in non‑convex models, and does not address how the analysis generalizes to such settings.
It is unclear why the proposed in‑support shifts would change the classification boundary; the definition of robustness central to the work is not provided.
The method for partitioning sketch images into ID and OOD subsets with respect to ImageNet is not explained, and the referenced Appendix B 3.2 does not exist.
The proposed intervention techniques at pre‑training and fine‑tuning on small, non‑diverse but debiased datasets are only cited without description, making the work not self‑contained.
The appendix is not separated from the main paper; the provided PDF is a 32‑page document that mixes both.

The contribution of the paper is unclear; both theoretical and empirical contributions are mild, and experiments in Section 6 do not clarify how small or non‑diverse the balanced dataset can be or the trade‑offs involved.

The theoretical analysis considers a very simple setting with an intuitive result and does not provide insights into the generalization behavior of models trained with pre‑training and balanced datasets, nor does it consider the effect of dataset size or diversity.

Out‑of‑support and in‑support are not formally defined; using a classifier to define these examples is problematic because the classifier’s decision boundary may not align with the true support of the distributions.
The central measure ER is not defined, and the connection between ER and MG (Figure 5 right) is unclear.

Practical implications are not well argued; the take‑aways may lack practical relevance, and the paper does not provide guidance on identifying out‑of‑support examples or creating a balanced dataset free of spurious correlations.
